query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Preheating the substrate and powder bed during the selective laser melting of AlCrFeNiSi feedstock will reduce thermal gradients, thereby minimizing residual stresses and enhancing microstructural homogeneity, which improves mechanical properties relative to components produced under conventional high-thermal-load conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: AlCrFeNiSi pre-alloyed, spherical powder feedstock intended for AM
generation.intervention: In situ substrate and powder bed preheating (e.g., to ~400°C) during the layer-by-layer build process
generation.conditions: Additive manufacturing using a selective laser melting process under a high-purity inert atmosphere on miniature component geometries; processing window similar to conventional conditions aside from the elevated base temperature; test conditions include mechanical evaluations at room temperature and up to ~700°C
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced thermal gradients during solidification lead to lower dislocation densities and more controlled precipitate formation at cell boundaries
generation.mechanism: By elevating the base temperature, the temperature differential between the melt pool and the substrate is decreased, which mitigates rapid contraction and associated high residual stresses. This controlled cooling minimizes non-equilibrium phase formation and promotes a more uniform microstructure that is beneficial for mechanical performance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Components manufactured with substrate preheating will exhibit significantly lower residual stresses, reduced microstructural defects (such as high dislocation densities and irregular precipitate distributions), and enhanced mechanical properties (e.g., improved yield strength and ductility) compared to those processed under conventional, ambient-temperature conditions.
generation.baseline: Components produced by conventional high-thermal-load additive manufacturing without substrate preheating, which typically show high residual stresses, degraded microstructural uniformity, and compromised mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This intervention is proposed for miniature component geometries produced via SLM using AlCrFeNiSi feedstock; its efficacy on larger components or different alloy systems remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The optimum preheat temperature and the quantitative extent of improvements in mechanical properties remain uncertain and may require iterative tuning.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of miniature AlCrFeNiSi components using SLM with all processing parameters identical except for the base temperature: one set with substrate preheating at ~400°C and a control set at ambient temperature. Characterize the microstructure, measure residual stresses, and perform mechanical testing (tensile/compression tests at room temperature and up to 700°C).
measurements: Dislocation density and precipitate morphology (via TEM/SEM)
Mechanical properties (yield strength, ultimate strength, ductility)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the components produced with substrate preheating do not exhibit statistically significant reductions in residual stress and improvements in microstructural uniformity and mechanical properties compared to the control group, or if unexpected degradation mechanisms are observed in the preheated group, then the hypothesis is falsified.

System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Selective laser melting (SLM) using pre-alloyed spherical powder (average diameter 27.2 µm); laser power 90 W, scan speed 600 mm/s, hatch space 80 µm, layer thickness 25 µm, volumetric energy density 75 J/mm³, 180° rotation scanning pattern, high-purity Ar atmosphere.. Test conditions: Compression tests at 25, 500, 600, 700, 800, and 900 °C; initial strain rate 1 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹; engineering strain limit 0.4; specimens preheated at 10 °C/min; MoS₂ lubricant used..
